stem: Where is Stonehenge?
explanation: Stonehenge is a famous prehistoric monument in Wiltshire, in the south-west of England. It was probably a special place for gatherings.

stem: Where is Skara Brae, a very well-preserved Stone Age village?
explanation: Skara Brae is on Orkney, off the north coast of Scotland. It is the best-preserved prehistoric village in northern Europe.

stem: In which year did the Romans, under Emperor Claudius, invade Britain?
explanation: Julius Caesar tried to invade in 55 BC but did not stay. The Romans returned under Emperor Claudius in AD 43 and ruled for about 400 years.

stem: Who was Boudicca?

options.label: Queen of the Iceni, who fought the Romans
A Roman empress who ruled Britain
A Saxon queen who defeated the Vikings

explanation: Boudicca led the Iceni, a tribe in what is now eastern England, against the Romans. Her statue stands on Westminster Bridge in London.

stem: Why did the Romans build Hadrian's Wall?

options.label: To keep out the Picts in the north
To mark the border with Wales
To protect London from the Saxons

explanation: Emperor Hadrian built the wall in the north of England to keep out the Picts, who were ancestors of the Scottish people.

stem: When did the Romans leave Britain?
explanation: The Roman army left Britain in AD 410 to defend other parts of the Roman Empire. They never returned.

stem: Which burial site in Suffolk held an Anglo-Saxon king, buried with treasure in a ship?
explanation: Sutton Hoo in Suffolk is the burial place of an Anglo-Saxon king. He was buried with treasure and armour, all placed inside a ship.

stem: Who became the first Archbishop of Canterbury?
explanation: St Augustine led missionaries from Rome who spread Christianity in the south of England. He became the first Archbishop of Canterbury.

stem: Where did the Vikings come from?
explanation: The Vikings came from Denmark and Norway. They first visited Britain in AD 789 to raid coastal towns and take goods and slaves.

stem: In which year did William of Normandy win the Battle of Hastings?
explanation: William defeated and killed the English king, Harold, at the Battle of Hastings in 1066. The battle is shown on the Bayeux Tapestry.

stem: After the Norman Conquest, William had a record made of towns, villages and land in England, called the Domesday Book.
explanation: The Domesday Book listed who owned land and what animals they had. It still exists and gives a picture of England after the Norman Conquest.

stem: Which Anglo-Saxon king united the kingdoms and defeated the Vikings?
explanation: Alfred the Great brought the Anglo-Saxon kingdoms together and defeated the Vikings. Many Vikings then settled in the east and north of England.

stem: About when did the first farmers arrive in Britain?
explanation: The first farmers arrived in Britain about 6,000 years ago. This marked the start of the Neolithic period, when people began to build permanent homes.

stem: Which metal was mixed with copper to make bronze in early Britain?
explanation: Around 2,100 BC, people in Britain learned to make bronze by mixing copper and tin. This period is known as the Bronze Age.

stem: What shape were the houses that people lived in during the Bronze Age?
explanation: During the Bronze Age, people lived in roundhouses. These homes were built with wooden poles, mud, and thatched roofs.

stem: In which English county is Maiden Castle, a huge Iron Age hill fort, located?
explanation: Maiden Castle is one of the largest and most famous Iron Age hill forts in Europe. It is located in Dorset, in the south of England.

stem: Who led the first, unsuccessful Roman invasions of Britain in 55 and 54 BC?
explanation: Julius Caesar led Roman armies to Britain in 55 and 54 BC, but he did not conquer the island. The successful invasion happened nearly 100 years later.

stem: Which language family was spoken by the people living in Britain during the Iron Age?
explanation: People in Iron Age Britain spoke Celtic languages. Today, modern languages like Welsh and Gaelic are part of this Celtic language family.

stem: Which Christian missionary travelled from Ireland to Scotland and founded a monastery on the island of Iona?
explanation: St Columba was an Irish monk who founded a famous monastery on Iona, an island off the coast of Scotland. He helped convert the Picts to Christianity.

stem: Where did Saint Patrick go as a missionary to spread Christianity, later becoming its patron saint?
explanation: Saint Patrick was born in Britain but went to Ireland as a missionary. He is now celebrated as the patron saint of Ireland.

stem: Which holy island off the northeast coast of England was raided by the Vikings in 793 AD?
explanation: The Vikings raided the monastery at Lindisfarne in 793 AD. This event is often seen as the start of the Viking Age in Britain.

stem: Which Danish king ruled England from 1016 to 1035 after years of conflict between Anglo-Saxons and Vikings?
explanation: King Cnut (also known as Canute) was a Danish king who became the sole ruler of England in 1016. His reign brought a period of peace.

stem: What is the Bayeux Tapestry?

options.label: An embroidery showing the Norman Conquest
A collection of old Anglo-Saxon laws
A map of Roman roads in Britain
A book of Viking religious stories

explanation: The Bayeux Tapestry is a long piece of embroidery made soon after 1066. It tells the story of the Norman Conquest of England.

stem: Which TWO Germanic tribes invaded and settled in Britain after the Roman army left?
explanation: After the Romans left in 410 AD, tribes from northern Europe invaded Britain. These included the Angles, Saxons, and Jutes.

stem: Which TWO of these were brought or heavily developed by the Romans during their rule in Britain?

options.label: The building of a road network
The introduction of new plants and animals
The building of the first hill forts

explanation: The Romans built a massive network of roads and introduced new crops, peas, and animals like rabbits to Britain. Hill forts were built earlier during the Iron Age.

stem: The Anglo-Saxons spoke a language that became the basis for modern English.
explanation: The Anglo-Saxons spoke dialects that developed into Old English. Many common words we use today come from this language.

stem: After the Norman Conquest of 1066, Norman French became the language of the king's court and the ruling class in England.
explanation: Following the Norman Conquest, Norman French became the language of government, parliament, and the upper classes. Many French words entered the English language as a result.

stem: When did Britain become an island separate from the continent of Europe?
explanation: Britain became an island around 10,000 years ago after the end of the last Ice Age, when rising sea levels created the English Channel.

stem: Which Anglo-Saxon king built a great wall of earth along the border with Wales?
explanation: King Offa of Mercia built a massive earthwork dyke along the Welsh border. Parts of Offa's Dyke can still be seen today.

stem: What was the name of the area in eastern and northern England where Viking laws applied?
explanation: The region ruled by Viking laws was known as the Danelaw. King Alfred defeated the Vikings and agreed to split England with them.

stem: Which king united the Gaelic and Pictish kingdoms to create Scotland in the 9th century?
explanation: In Scotland, Kenneth MacAlpin united the Scots and the Picts into one kingdom during the 9th century, laying the foundation for modern Scotland.

stem: Under the feudal system introduced by William the Conqueror, what was given in return for land?
explanation: Under the feudal system, the king gave land to his lords in exchange for military service and loyalty.

stem: Approximately how long did the Roman period in Britain last?
explanation: The Romans ruled Britain for nearly 400 years, from AD 43 until they left in AD 410 to defend Rome.

stem: During the Bronze Age, what circular earth mounds were built to bury important people?
explanation: Bronze Age people buried their dead in round barrows with pottery, metal objects, and ornaments.

stem: What name did the Romans give to the ancient tribes in northern Scotland who painted their bodies?
explanation: The Romans called the people in northern Scotland the Picts, which means 'painted people', because they decorated their bodies.

stem: Which English king was killed at the Battle of Hastings in 1066?
explanation: King Harold was killed at the Battle of Hastings in 1066, leading to the conquest of England by William, Duke of Normandy.

stem: What major development in money occurred in Britain during the Iron Age?
explanation: During the Iron Age, people in Britain began minting their own coins, often stamped with the names of local kings.

stem: Which TWO armies fought each other at the Battle of Hastings in 1066?
explanation: The Battle of Hastings was fought in 1066 between the Anglo-Saxon army led by King Harold and the Norman invaders led by William, Duke of Normandy.

stem: In which TWO parts of the United Kingdom are Celtic languages still spoken today?
explanation: Celtic languages survived in western and northern regions. Today, Welsh is spoken in Wales and Gaelic is spoken in Scotland.

stem: Which TWO of these were introduced or made in Britain during the Iron Age?
explanation: During the Iron Age, people learned how to work with iron to make weapons and tools, and built hilltop forts for defence. Stonehenge was built earlier.

stem: The Romans successfully conquered all of Scotland and kept control of it throughout their rule.
explanation: The Romans were unable to conquer the tribes in northern Scotland. They built Hadrian's Wall and Antonine's Wall to mark their northern border.

stem: The Domesday Book was written in Anglo-Saxon English.
explanation: The Domesday Book was written in Latin, which was the official language used for public documents in England after the Norman Conquest.

stem: Who was the first recorded Christian martyr in Britain?
explanation: St Alban was a Roman soldier who became a Christian. He was executed by the Romans for his faith and became Britain's first Christian martyr.

stem: Where was William the Conqueror crowned King of England on Christmas Day 1066?
explanation: William the Conqueror was crowned at Westminster Abbey in London. This tradition of crowning monarchs there continues today.

stem: How did the first people in Britain get their food during the Stone Age?

options.label: By hunting animals and gathering wild plants
By importing grain from mainland Europe
By growing wheat in large open fields
By keeping herds of cows in wooden barns

explanation: The earliest people in Britain were hunter-gatherers. They followed herds of wild animals like deer and horses, and collected wild fruit and nuts.

stem: In which year did Saint Augustine arrive in Britain to spread Christianity to the Anglo-Saxons?
explanation: Pope Gregory the Great sent Saint Augustine to Britain in 597 AD. He became the first Archbishop of Canterbury and helped convert the south of England.

stem: Around how many years ago did the Bronze Age begin in Britain?
explanation: The Bronze Age started around 4,000 years ago (2,000 BC) when people learned to make bronze. The Stone Age came before it, and the Iron Age came after.

stem: What was the main occupation for most people living in Britain during the Iron Age?
explanation: Most people in the Iron Age were farmers. Others were craft workers, like potters and metalworkers, or warriors who defended their tribes.

stem: Which Anglo-Saxon kingdom did King Alfred the Great rule?
explanation: King Alfred the Great was the ruler of Wessex, the only Anglo-Saxon kingdom that successfully resisted the Viking invasions.

stem: Which TWO of the following were Anglo-Saxon kingdoms in Britain?
explanation: The Anglo-Saxons established several kingdoms in Britain, including Wessex, Mercia, Northumbria, and Kent. Normandy and Brittany are regions in France.

stem: Which TWO modern British cities were first established as important towns by the Romans?
explanation: The Romans established many cities during their 400-year rule, including London (Londinium) and York (Eboracum), which were connected by roads.

stem: The Norman Conquest of 1066 was the last successful foreign invasion of England.
explanation: The Norman Conquest of 1066 was the last successful invasion of England. Since then, no foreign army has successfully conquered the country.
